title: Doctrine of Proportionality in Administrative Law

content.overview: Proportionality is a structured standard of review that asks whether an administrative measure is suitable, necessary and balanced in relation to its legitimate aim. Indian courts apply it with greater intensity where fundamental rights or severe burdens are engaged, while retaining Wednesbury unreasonableness for ordinary administrative discretion.
content.glance: Identify the aim and the measure; test suitability, necessity (least restrictive means) and balance (proportionality stricto sensu); state the intensity of review appropriate to the context.
content.study: Proportionality provides a more structured alternative or complement to classical Wednesbury unreasonableness. The inquiry typically examines whether the measure pursues a legitimate aim, whether it is suitable to achieve that aim, whether a less restrictive means was available, and whether the burden imposed is disproportionate to the benefit. Intensity of review varies with the nature of the right and the institutional competence of the decision-maker. Current-law framing: ground the analysis in Article 14/19/21 context and the specific administrative measure.

sections.heading: Meaning and Structure
sections.body: Suitability, necessity and balance form the core structured inquiry.

sections.heading: Relationship with Wednesbury
sections.body: Wednesbury asks whether the decision is so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could reach it; proportionality is a structured means-ends analysis. Both are used in Indian law depending on context.

sections.heading: Intensity of Review
sections.body: Higher intensity where fundamental rights or severe interests are engaged; greater deference for pure policy or polycentric decisions.

sections.heading: Application
sections.body: Identify aim, measure, alternatives and balance; avoid substituting the court’s preferred policy outcome.

examples.title: Blanket ban
examples.body: An authority imposes a complete ban on an activity to address a limited risk where a narrower restriction would suffice. Necessity (least restrictive means) is engaged.

examples.title: Ordinary licensing discretion
examples.body: A licensing authority refuses a licence on fitness grounds within a range of reasonable options. Classical Wednesbury may be the appropriate intensity rather than full structured proportionality.

hypotheticals.question: Is proportionality identical to Wednesbury?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Proportionality is structured (suitability, necessity, balance); Wednesbury is a high-threshold unreasonableness test. Context determines which is applied.

hypotheticals.question: Does proportionality allow the court to redecide policy?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. It tests the relationship between means and ends; it does not substitute the court’s preferred policy.

rows.right: No reasonable authority could reach the decision

misconceptions.trap: Proportionality is the same as Wednesbury.
misconceptions.correction: They are distinct standards; intensity and structure differ.

misconceptions.trap: Proportionality always requires the court to choose the least restrictive option itself.
misconceptions.correction: The court tests whether the authority’s choice was proportionate; it does not assume the primary policy role.

cases.name: Om Kumar v Union of India
cases.facts: Disciplinary and administrative measures raising the standard of review.
cases.issue: When proportionality applies to administrative action.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Proportionality is applicable in appropriate contexts, particularly where rights are engaged; Wednesbury remains relevant for ordinary administrative discretion.
cases.relevance: Leading Indian authority on proportionality in administrative law.

cases.name: Tata Cellular v Union of India
cases.issue: Scope of review of administrative discretion.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Courts review legality and rationality without substituting commercial judgment.
cases.relevance: Framework for intensity of review of administrative action.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a proportionality problem be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Identify aim and measure. II. Test suitability, necessity and balance. III. State the appropriate intensity. IV. Conclude without substituting policy.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What should submissions contain?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Aim and measure; structured proportionality analysis; intensity justification; precise relief.
